script.opening: "Doctor, I've got a problem with my right knee and I have to be honest with you — I don't want to be told to stop. I've got Wainwright's Coast-to-Coast booked in two months."

facts.text: Aching medial knee pain, worse going downhill and on stairs. Six weeks. No swelling, no locking, no giving way. Stiff for ~15 mins in the morning.
Can walk 6 miles before the pain becomes limiting. Used to do 15 without issue.
Mild osteoarthritis confirmed in his left knee 4 years ago, settled with physiotherapy.
Paracetamol — minimal effect. Ibuprofen gel — some help. Stopped using his walking poles a year ago because "he didn't need them".
This walk is in memory of his late wife, who he had planned to do it with. He has trained for nine months. He is doing it alone.
If GP listens, he opens up about loneliness since wife's death and how this walk is what is keeping him going.

ice.ideas: Thinks it's "wear and tear" but expects an injection that will fix it.
ice.concerns: Genuinely afraid of being told to cancel. Wants to honour his wife.
ice.expectations: A steroid injection or strong painkillers to get him through the walk.

cues: Photo of late wife — he holds it up to the camera.
Says "Margaret would have hated me to give up".
Looks visibly distressed if you suggest cancelling.

checkpoints.text: Asks for the knee examination findings (effusion, ROM, joint-line tenderness, McMurray, ligaments) — provided on request, as in the exam
Recognises probable medial-compartment OA — does not arrange MRI or X-ray reflexively
Offers structured non-operative plan: weight, quads strengthening, topical NSAID, paracetamol, poles, downhill technique
Discusses oral NSAID risk in older patient on statin, offers PPI cover if needed
Acknowledges the meaning of the walk — Margaret, grief, what completing it would mean
Negotiates: doesn't order him to cancel; offers a graded plan with check-in at 4 weeks
Safety-nets red flags: sudden swelling, locking, giving way, systemic symptoms

worked.txt: "Donald — before we talk about the knee, tell me about the walk. Why this one, why now?"
"I can hear that this is for Margaret as much as it is for you. Let's see what we can do to get you on that path."
"This looks like wear-and-tear in the inner side of the knee. That doesn't mean you can't walk — but it does mean we need to load the knee differently."
"I don't want to tell you to cancel. I want us to write a four-week plan and see what the knee does. If it gets worse, we re-talk. Deal?"
"There's a charity called Cruse that helps with the kind of long road you're on — would you like me to send the link?"

f.learning: OA in primary care is non-operative and patient-centred. The marking gap is rarely the medicine — it's noticing the bereavement subtext, naming what the walk means, and negotiating rather than dictating. Imaging adds nothing when the diagnosis is clear and surgery is not the answer.

knowledge.summary: Osteoarthritis is a clinical diagnosis; imaging is not needed when the picture is typical. Management is non-operative and centres on exercise and weight, with topical NSAIDs first-line.

points.t: Activity-related joint pain in someone ≥45 with morning stiffness ≤30 min needs no X-ray to diagnose OA. Image only if it would change management or red flags suggest another cause.
Therapeutic exercise (muscle strengthening + aerobic) and weight loss if overweight are the cornerstones — offered to everyone, not as a last resort.

Topical NSAID first-line for knee OA. Oral NSAID at lowest effective dose for shortest time + PPI cover; weigh GI/renal/CV risk. NICE NG226: do not routinely offer paracetamol or weak opioids (only infrequent short-term use when all else is unsuitable); never strong opioids or glucosamine.

Walking aids/poles, appropriate footwear, and pacing/technique advice (e.g. downhill loading). Consider an intra-articular steroid when other drugs are ineffective or unsuitable, or to support exercise — relief is short-term (about 2–10 weeks).
Refer for surgical opinion when symptoms substantially affect quality of life and non-surgical management has failed — not on X-ray appearance alone.
Hot swollen joint, locking, true giving-way, systemic upset or trauma needs reassessment.

model.text: Morning Donald, come in — have a seat. What’s brought you along today?
It’s my right knee, doc. Been aching for months. I’m a keen hill walker and it’s really starting to get in the way.
That sounds frustrating, especially with the walking. Tell me more about the pain — when it’s worst and how it behaves.
Worse after a long walk, and going downhill. Stiff for about ten minutes when I get up, then it eases.
Any swelling, locking, or does it ever give way under you?
model.why: Targeted questions to separate OA from mechanical/inflammatory causes

model.text: A bit puffy sometimes after a big walk. No real locking or giving way.
Any pain in the hip or the back, and is the other knee okay?
Hip’s fine, back’s fine. Left knee twinges occasionally but nothing like this.
Has it been hot, red or suddenly swollen, and have you felt at all unwell or feverish with it?
No, nothing like that. Just the wear-and-tear ache.
And in terms of your general health — any other conditions, and what medication are you on?
Just cholesterol tablets. Atorvastatin. Otherwise fit as a fiddle, that’s why this is bugging me.
Before we go further — what do you think is going on in there, and is there anything in particular you’re worried about?
I reckon it’s bone on bone. My mate had that and needed a full knee replacement — I’m dreading being told I need one, and being off my feet for months.
Thank you — that helps me a lot. And what were you hoping we could do today?
Honestly, I half expected you’d send me for a scan to see how bad it is.

Let me examine the knee — I’ll look at it, feel for warmth and swelling, and check how it moves and bears weight. (Examines.) Good news: it’s not hot or hugely swollen, the movement’s reasonable, and it’s stable.
model.why: Focused examination and interprets the findings

model.text: So what is it then?

From the pattern — your age, activity-related pain, brief morning stiffness, and the exam — this is osteoarthritis. And here’s the key thing: when it’s this typical, we diagnose it clinically. An X-ray rarely changes what we do, and the picture on the scan often doesn’t match the pain anyway, so I wouldn’t routinely send you.
model.why: Reaches the diagnosis and correctly avoids unnecessary imaging

model.text: Oh — I assumed a scan was the whole point.

It’s a really common assumption. Let me reassure you on the big fear too: “bone on bone” doesn’t automatically mean a replacement. Most people manage well for years without surgery — and staying active actually protects the joint rather than wearing it out.

The treatment with the best evidence isn’t a tablet — it’s exercise to strengthen the muscles around the knee, plus, if you’re open to it, a little weight loss to offload it. I can refer you to a physiotherapist to get you a tailored programme. How does that land?
I can do exercise — I just don’t want to make it worse.

You won’t — soreness that settles is fine and expected. For the pain, I’d start with a topical anti-inflammatory gel rather than tablets, because it’s effective for knees and much safer on the stomach and kidneys. If you need something stronger for a flare, a short course of an anti-inflammatory with a stomach-protecting tablet — though we’d be a bit cautious given your age. I’d steer away from strong painkillers like codeine.
model.why: Stepwise analgesia tailored safely to comorbidity

model.text: That all sounds sensible.

And to be clear about surgery: we’d consider a referral for a surgical opinion only if your quality of life is really suffering despite all this — not on the basis of a scan. So the path is in your hands.

Safety-net: if the knee ever becomes hot, very swollen and painful, especially with feeling unwell, that needs urgent review — that’s not ordinary arthritis. Otherwise let’s review in six weeks to see how the exercises and gel are going. Can you tell me back the plan as you understand it?
model.why: Red-flag safety-net, defined follow-up, checks understanding

model.text: Physio and exercises, lose a bit of weight, gel for the pain, stronger stuff only for a flare, and back in six weeks. And no, I don’t need a replacement just yet.
Perfect summary — and you’ve clearly taken the reassuring part on board, which I’m really pleased about.

Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

playbook.diagnosis: State it plainly and reassure: “From your age, the activity-related pain and brief morning stiffness, this is osteoarthritis. When it’s this typical we diagnose it clinically — an X-ray rarely changes what we do.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Osteoarthritis is the normal wear and tear of a well-used joint — like the tread on a favourite pair of walking boots. ‘Bone on bone’ sounds frightening, but it doesn’t mean you need a new knee, and staying active actually protects it.”

management.reflectIce: “You were dreading being told you need a replacement like your mate — let me reassure you: most people manage well for years without surgery, and we decide that on how you’re living, never on a scan.”
management.psychosocial: Anchor the plan to getting him back on the hills — exercise as treatment (not rest), and a little weight loss framed as offloading the joint for longer walks.

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed on the scan negotiation and lecture-mode lifestyle advice — almost never on osteoarthritis knowledge.

items.fail: Ordering an X-ray “to confirm” typical OA — or an MRI — because that is what the patient came for.
items.why: NICE NG226: activity-related pain at ≥45 with stiffness under 30 minutes is a clinical diagnosis. Routine imaging is a classic habit from systems where scans are defensive practice — “investigations not in line with UK practice”.
items.fix: Diagnose clinically with confidence and explain the why: “When the picture is this typical, an X-ray doesn’t change what we do — and it can’t measure pain.”

items.fail: Dismissing the scan expectation flat — “you don’t need one” — and moving on.
items.why: “Does not address the patient’s expectation.” Refusing without negotiating throws away the Relating marks the expectation exists to test.
items.fix: Acknowledge, explain, and leave the door open: “If we’ve strengthened that leg for six weeks and you’re no better, an X-ray is absolutely still on the table.”

items.fail: “You need to lose weight and exercise more” delivered as a verdict.
items.why: “Management plan generic and not negotiated” — and weight raised as blame is the most common Relating failure in lifestyle-heavy stations.
items.fix: Anchor everything to his identity: “My job is to get you back up the hills. Strengthening the muscle around the knee is the best treatment we have — and a little weight off is a lighter rucksack on every step.”

items.fail: Paracetamol-and-rest as the plan — or reaching for codeine.
items.why: NG226 de-emphasises paracetamol and weak opioids, and rest worsens OA — “management not in line with current best practice”.
items.fix: Topical NSAID first-line for the knee; a short oral NSAID course with PPI cover for flares (respecting age, renal and CV risk); exercise prescribed as the treatment, not the fallback.

items.fail: “Wear and tear… bone on bone” — the harmful imagery used by the doctor, or left unchallenged.
items.why: “Explanation likely to increase anxiety.” His fear of a knee replacement comes from exactly that picture.
items.fix: Reframe it: “Joints are built to be used — think tread on a well-loved boot, not bone grinding on bone. Most people with this never need surgery.”

items.fail: Pain discussed, life not — no functional goal, no review, no red flags.
items.why: “Plan lacked follow-up or a measurable outcome.” Examiners want a goal the patient cares about.
items.fix: Set it together — “a comfortable five-mile walk in six weeks” — refer physio/ESCAPE-pain, book the review, and name the hot-swollen-joint red flags.

timeMap.d: He declares the agenda himself: "don't tell me to stop." Ask about the walk before the knee — the why matters more than the joint.

Mechanical screen: locking, giving way, swelling, morning stiffness, walking distance. Ask for the examination findings — they're provided on request. Probe what the walk means — Margaret surfaces here.
"This behaves like wear-and-tear in the inner half of the knee — and I've heard why this walk can't simply be cancelled."
Graded plan: quads work, poles back, downhill technique, topical NSAID ± oral with PPI cover, weight conversation handled kindly. A 4-week check-in, not a verdict.
Red flags: sudden swelling, locking, giving way, systemic symptoms. Tactful bereavement signpost (Cruse). Deal confirmed.

wordPics.fail: Orders an X-ray or MRI reflexively and hides behind it; tells him to cancel the walk; never asks why the walk matters, so Margaret never comes up; management is "painkillers and rest"; no review point.
wordPics.pass: Recognises medial-compartment OA clinically; gives a structured non-operative plan; doesn't forbid the walk; acknowledges the bereavement once it surfaces; sets a review and basic red-flag safety-net.
wordPics.exc: Asks about the walk before the knee, so the grief story arrives early and shapes everything; negotiates a written 4-week graded plan with an explicit re-talk point; handles weight and NSAID risk without preaching; signposts Cruse so it lands as care, not dismissal.

avoid.dont: "At your age, some wear and tear is to be expected."
avoid.instead: "This looks like wear-and-tear in the inner side of the knee — which we can work with. It does not automatically mean stopping."
avoid.why: "At your age" patronises and closes the conversation.

avoid.dont: "I really think you should consider cancelling the walk."
avoid.instead: "I don't want to cancel anything today. I want a four-week plan and an honest check-in — then we decide together."
avoid.why: Dictating loses the negotiation mark and the patient.

avoid.dont: "We'll get an X-ray and take it from there."
avoid.instead: "An X-ray wouldn't change what we do next — the diagnosis is clinical and the plan starts today."
avoid.why: Reflex imaging signals you don't know the OA guidance.

items.fail: Dismissing the scan expectation flat — “you don’t need one” — and moving on.
items.why: “Does not address the patient’s expectation.” Refusing without negotiating throws away the Relating marks the expectation exists to test.
items.fix: Acknowledge, explain, and leave the door open: “If we’ve strengthened that leg for six weeks and you’re no better, an X-ray is absolutely still on the table.”

items.fail: “You need to lose weight and exercise more” delivered as a verdict.
items.why: “Management plan generic and not negotiated” — and weight raised as blame is the most common Relating failure in lifestyle-heavy stations.
items.fix: Anchor everything to his identity: “My job is to get you back up the hills. Strengthening the muscle around the knee is the best treatment we have — and a little weight off is a lighter rucksack on every step.”

items.fail: Paracetamol-and-rest as the plan — or reaching for codeine.
items.why: NG226 de-emphasises paracetamol and weak opioids, and rest worsens OA — “management not in line with current best practice”.
items.fix: Topical NSAID first-line for the knee; a short oral NSAID course with PPI cover for flares (respecting age, renal and CV risk); exercise prescribed as the treatment, not the fallback.

items.fail: “Wear and tear… bone on bone” — the harmful imagery used by the doctor, or left unchallenged.
items.why: “Explanation likely to increase anxiety.” His fear of a knee replacement comes from exactly that picture.
items.fix: Reframe it: “Joints are built to be used — think tread on a well-loved boot, not bone grinding on bone. Most people with this never need surgery.”

items.fail: Pain discussed, life not — no functional goal, no review, no red flags.
items.why: “Plan lacked follow-up or a measurable outcome.” Examiners want a goal the patient cares about.
items.fix: Set it together — “a comfortable five-mile walk in six weeks” — refer physio/ESCAPE-pain, book the review, and name the hot-swollen-joint red flags.
